title: Administrative Tribunals — Structure, Powers and Procedure

content.overview: The structure, powers and procedure of administrative tribunals are fixed by their parent statutes and by constitutional requirements of independence and judicial review. Appointment, tenure, jurisdiction, powers to summon evidence and appellate hierarchies must be examined together.
content.glance: Map the statutory structure (appointment, tenure, benches, powers, appeals); test independence; identify the judicial-review route to the High Court or Supreme Court.
content.study: Structural legitimacy of tribunals depends on how members are appointed and removed, the security of tenure, the separation of administrative control from adjudicatory function, and the preservation of judicial review under Articles 226/227 and 32. Powers to regulate procedure, summon witnesses and enforce orders are statutory. Defective structure can invite constitutional challenge even if individual decisions appear fair. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the parent statute and Constitution. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Appointment and Tenure
sections.body: Method of appointment and security of tenure affect independence.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Powers
sections.body: Defined by the parent Act; includes procedural and enforcement powers as conferred.

sections.heading: Independence Requirements
sections.body: Freedom from executive control over adjudicatory outcomes.

sections.heading: Judicial Review
sections.body: High Court and Supreme Court supervision cannot be wholly excluded.

examples.title: Structural challenge
examples.body: Appointment rules place adjudicatory members under pervasive executive control. A structural challenge to independence is open even without attacking a particular order.

examples.title: Finality and review
examples.body: Parent Act says tribunal orders are final. High Court review under Articles 226/227 remains available per L. Chandra Kumar.

hypotheticals.question: If the statute says the tribunal is final, can High Courts interfere?
Does any executive role in appointments destroy the tribunal?
hypotheticals.analysis: The test is overall independence, not the total absence of any executive role.

distinctions.title: Structural challenge vs challenge to individual order
distinctions.left: Attack on design of the tribunal
distinctions.right: Attack on a particular decision's legality or fairness

misconceptions.trap: If the statute says the tribunal is final, High Courts cannot interfere.
Any executive role in appointments destroys the tribunal.
misconceptions.correction: The test is overall independence, not the total absence of any executive role.

cases.name: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India
cases.facts: Constitutional validity of the tribunal system and exclusion of High Court jurisdiction.
cases.issue: What is the constitutional place of tribunals and judicial review by High Courts?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Tribunals may perform specialised functions, but decisions remain subject to High Court review under Articles 226/227.
cases.holding: Tribunals upheld subject to constitutional judicial review.
cases.relevance: Leading authority on structure and review.

cases.name: Union of India v Madras Bar Association
cases.issue: What institutional safeguards are required for constitutionally valid tribunals?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Tribunalisation must preserve independence, impartiality and adjudicatory standards.
cases.relevance: Authority already in the file on composition and independence.

cases.name: Rojer Mathew v South Indian Bank Ltd.
cases.facts: Tribunal conditions of service rules examined.
cases.issue: Whether tribunal service conditions could be structured inconsistently with judicial independence.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Tribunal administration must conform to constitutional independence requirements.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a tribunals-structure problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Map statutory structure. II. Test independence. III. Identify review route. IV. Formulate structural or individual relief.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Structure mapped; independence analysis; review pathway; precise relief.

examTips: Separate structural challenges from challenges to individual orders.
